Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 1:

(p-458) Surat al-Mu'minun is Meccan, and it has one hundred and eighteen verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾ "Qad" here is the opposite of "lamma": "qad" affirms what is expected, while "lamma" negates it. The believers had been expecting this kind of good news, which is the announcement that success is established for them. So they were addressed with something that indicates the establishment of what they had been expecting. Al-falah (success) is attaining what is sought and being saved from what is feared; that is, they have achieved what they sought, or they have been saved from what they fled. Al-iman (faith) linguistically means tasdiq (affirmation, belief), and the mu'min (believer) is one who affirms. In the Shari'ah, it is whoever utters the two testimonies while his heart agrees with his tongue, and such a person is a believer. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah created Paradise and said to it, 'Speak!' It said, 'The believers have indeed succeeded,' three times. [Then Allah said:] 'I am forbidden to every stingy person who shows off.'" Because showing off (riya') nullifies the bodily acts of worship, and he has no act of worship involving wealth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 2:

﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾ — fearful in the heart, still in the limbs. It has also been said: humility (khushu') in prayer is gathering one's resolve (himmah) for it and turning away from everything other than it, not letting one's gaze pass beyond its place of prostration (musalla), not turning about, not playing with anything, not drawing the lower garment over oneself (al-sadl), not cracking one's fingers, not fidgeting with pebbles, and the like. And it is narrated from Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) that it is: sincerity of speech, reverence for the station (of standing before Allah), complete certainty, and full concentration of attention. The prayer is attributed to those who pray (al-musallin) and not to the One to whom prayer is offered (al-musalla lahu), because the benefit of prayer belongs to the one who prays alone; it is his provision and his store. As for the One to whom prayer is offered, He is free of need of it.

Surah 23, verse 3 — Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil)

﴿And those who turn away from idle talk,﴾

Al-laghw (idle talk, vain speech) is every utterance that is worthless and ought to be discarded, such as lying, insult and frivolous jesting. The meaning is that they have such earnestness that it preoccupies them away from frivolity. When He described them with humility in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from idle talk, so as to combine for them the two demanding acts upon the self, doing and refraining, which are the two foundations upon which the building of moral obligation (taklif) rests.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 4:

﴿And those who are active in giving zakah﴾ (mu'addun, "those who pay"). The word fa'iluna ("active in") indicates continuity and constancy, unlike mu'addun ("paying").

It has been said that zakah (zakah, the obligatory alms) is a homonym (ism mushtarak) which is applied to the thing itself, namely the amount that the one who pays zakah removes from the nisab (nisab, the minimum threshold of wealth liable for zakah) and gives to the poor (faqir). It is also applied to the meaning, namely the act of the one who pays zakah, which is purification (tazkiyah). This is what is intended here. Thus He made those who purify (al-muzakkin) "doers" of it, because the word "act" (fi'l) encompasses all acts, such as striking (darb), killing (qatl) and the like. You say to the one who strikes, the one who kills, and the one who purifies: "He did the striking, the killing, and the purifying (al-tazkiyah)."

It is also permissible that zakah be understood as the thing itself, with an omitted genitive construction (mudaf mahdhuf) being assumed, namely "payment" (al-ada'). The preposition lam (li-) is used here because the object is placed first (taqaddum al-maf'ul) and because the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is weak in governing (di'f ism al-fa'il fi al-'amal). For you say: "This is one who strikes for Zayd (hadha darib li-Zayd)," and you do not say: "He struck for Zayd (darab li-Zayd)."
**Verse 5 of Surah al-Mu'minun (23):** ﴿And those who guard their private parts,﴾ — al-Farj (the private part) includes the nakedness (sawʾah) of both the man and the woman.

[Page 460] ﴿except with their spouses﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is, [it means] except while being governors over their spouses or guardians over them, from your saying: "Ziyād was over Basra," meaning he was its governor. The meaning is: they guard their private parts in all circumstances, except in the circumstance of marrying or taking concubines. Or ﴿ʿalā﴾ is connected to an elided element indicated by ﴿not blameworthy﴾, as if it were said: "they are blamed," ﴿except with their spouses﴾, meaning: they are blamed for every act of intimacy except what has been permitted to them, for they are not blameworthy for it. Al-Farrāʾ said: ﴿except from their spouses﴾, meaning their wives. ﴿Or what their right hands possess﴾, meaning their female slaves. He did not say "min" (from) because the slave is treated like non-rational beings, and for this reason he is sold as cattle are sold. ﴿Then they are not blameworthy﴾, meaning there is no blame upon them if they do not guard their private parts from their wives and their female slaves.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 7:

﴿So whoever seeks beyond that﴾ seeks the satisfaction of desire from other than these two ﴿those are the transgressors﴾ the ones who are complete in transgression (al-'udwan). And in it is evidence for the prohibition of mut'ah (temporary pleasure) and of seeking enjoyment by means of the hand (al-kaff) in order to satisfy desire.

The commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 23, verse 8:

﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their covenant,﴾ "لِأمانَتِهِمْ" (*li-amanatihim*, in the singular "their trust") is read by Makki (the reading of Ibn Kathir of Mecca, a *qira'a*, or canonical variant recitation) and Sahl, and it is easy. He called the thing entrusted and the thing covenanted upon "amanah" (trust) and "ahd" (covenant). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render back the trusts to their owners﴾ [an-Nisa: 58]. What is rendered back is the physical objects, not the meanings. The intended meaning is general, covering everything they were entrusted with and everything they were bound to, whether from Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, or from the creation. ﴿Keepers﴾ means guarding. The *ra'i* (shepherd, one who oversees) is the one who stands over a thing with guarding and reforming, like the shepherd of sheep.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 9:

﴿And those who are over their prayers﴾ "ṣalātihim" (their prayers) is read in the Kufan reading (qirā'a) except by Abu Bakr, ﴿they guard﴾ (yuḥāfiẓūn), meaning they persist in performing them at their appointed times. The repetition of the mention of the prayer is because it is more important, and because humility (khushū') in it is other than merely guarding it. Or, because it was first mentioned in the singular so that humility is conveyed for the category of prayer, any prayer whatsoever, and then mentioned in the plural at the end so that guarding over its types is conveyed: the obligatory (farā'iḍ), the required (wājibāt), the sunnah prayers (sunan), and the voluntary prayers (nawāfil).

Those (﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾) who combine these attributes, ﴿they are the inheritors﴾, deserving to be called inheritors (wurrath) to the exclusion of all others. Then he (al-Nasafi) introduced the heading "the inheritors" with his statement:

﴿Those who will inherit﴾ from the disbelievers. In a hadith: "There is none among you but that he has two abodes: an abode in Paradise and an abode in the Fire. If he dies and enters Paradise, the people of the Fire inherit his abode; and if he dies and enters the Fire, the people of Paradise inherit his abode." ﴿Firdaws﴾ is the wide garden containing all kinds of fruit. Qutrub said it is the highest of the gardens. ﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾. He made the feminine pronoun agree with Firdaws by interpreting it as Paradise (al-Jannah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 12:

﴿And We certainly created man﴾, i.e., Adam, ﴿from an extract of clay﴾. Min (from) here indicates the starting point (li-l-ibtida'). Sulala (extract) means the best part, because it is drawn out (tusall) from among the turbidity (al-kadar). It is also said that the dust from which Adam was created was called sulala only because it was extracted (subbira) from every kind of soil. ﴿from clay﴾. Min (from) here indicates explanation (li-l-bayan), as in His saying ﴿from the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 13:

﴿Then We made it﴾ i.e., its offspring (naslahu), so the modified noun (al-mudaf) was elided and the modifier (al-mudaf ilayhi) was put in its place, because Adam (peace be upon him) did not become a drop (nutfah). It is like His saying: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7], ﴿then He made his offspring from an extract of a liquid, despised﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8]. It has also been said that "man" (al-insan) means the children of Adam, and "extract" (al-sulalah) is the drop (nutfah), and the Arabs call the drop "sulalah." So the meaning is: ﴿And We created man from an extract﴾, i.e., from a drop extracted (maslulah) from clay, i.e., from a creature made of clay, who is Adam (peace be upon him). ﴿A drop﴾ (nutfah), i.e., a small amount of water, ﴿in a firm place﴾ (qarar), i.e., a settled place, meaning the womb, ﴿secure﴾ (makin), i.e., well-protected.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 14:**

﴿Then We made the drop of semen into a clinging clot, then We made the clinging clot into a lump of flesh.﴾ ﴿Then We made the drop of semen﴾, meaning: We transformed it. The evidence is that the verb (khalaqa) is transitive to two objects, whereas khalq (creating) is transitive to one object. ﴿A clinging clot﴾, a piece of blood. The meaning is: We changed the white drop of semen into a red clot. ﴿Then We made the clinging clot into a lump of flesh﴾, flesh in the amount that can be chewed. ﴿Then We made the lump of flesh into bones﴾, meaning We transformed it into bones. ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾, meaning We made flesh grow over them, so that it became for them like a garment. The reading "al-ʿaẓma" (the singular, with the definite article) is that of Ibn ʿĀmir (Shami) and Abu Bakr, and "ʿaẓman" (singular, indefinite) is that of Abu Zayd from Yaʿqub. The reading "al-ʿiẓāma" (plural, definite) is that of Zayd from Yaʿqub, and "ʿiẓāman" (plural, indefinite) is that of Abu Zayd. The singular is used in place of the plural because there is no ambiguity, since the human being has many bones. ﴿Then We brought him into being as another creation﴾. The pronoun refers to the human being, or to what was mentioned. ﴿Another creation﴾, meaning a creation distinct from the first creation, since He made him an animal when he was inanimate, and speaking, hearing and seeing, when he had the opposite of these attributes. For this reason we say: if someone usurps an egg and it hatches in his possession, he must compensate for the egg and does not return the chick, because it is a creation other than the egg. ﴿So blessed is Allah﴾, meaning exalted is His command in His power and knowledge. ﴿The best﴾ (aḥsan) is either an apposition (badal) or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'). It is not an adjective (ṣifa), because it is indefinite (nakira), even though it is grammatically annexed (uḍīfa), since the annexed noun is a substitute for "min" (of, i.e., a partitive). ﴿Of the creators﴾, meaning the ones who determine (or measure). The meaning is: the best of those who determine in determining. The specifying noun (tamyīz) is omitted because "the creators" indicates it. It has been said that ʿAbd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, the scribe of the Prophet ﷺ, uttered this phrase before the Prophet dictated it to him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him, "Thus was it revealed." ʿAbd Allah said: "If Muhammad is a prophet to whom revelation is sent, then I am a prophet to whom revelation is sent." He apostatized and joined Mecca, then he embraced Islam again on the day of the Conquest. It has also been said that this report is not authentic, because his apostasy took place in Medina, and this surah is Meccan. It has also been said that the one who said it was ʿUmar or Muʿadh, may Allah be pleased with them both.
Then indeed you, after that (ba'da dhalika), after what We have mentioned of your condition, are surely dying (la-mayyitun), at the expiry of your terms.
Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised up (tub'athun). You will come to life for the recompense.

**Quranic verse (23:17):** ﴿And We have certainly created above you seven paths.﴾

The word ﴿طَرائِقَ﴾ (ṭarā’iq) is the plural of ﴿طَرِيقَةٍ﴾ (ṭarīqa), and it refers to the heavens. It is as if He said: "We created them above you, and We were not unmindful of their preservation." Alternatively, the word refers to people, meaning that He created the heavens above them only so that He might open to them provisions and blessings from them, and He was not unmindful of them or of what sets them right.

(p-463)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 18:

﴿And We sent down water from the sky﴾ in measure, ﴿in a measured amount﴾, by a determined quantity whereby they are safe from harm and reach benefit; or in the amount of what We knew of their needs. ﴿Then We made it settle in the earth﴾, like His saying ﴿then He threaded it as springs in the earth﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. It was also said: We made it stable in the earth, so all the water of the earth comes from the sky. Then He demanded their gratitude with His saying ﴿And indeed, We are able to take it away﴾, i.e., just as We were able to send it down, We are able to take it away; so bind this blessing with gratitude.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 19:

﴿So We brought forth for you thereby﴾ — by the water — ﴿gardens of date-palms﴾ ﴿and grapevines; in them﴾ — in the gardens — ﴿are many fruits﴾ besides the date-palms and the grapevines ﴿and from them you eat﴾. That is: from the gardens, that is: from their fruits. It is also permissible that this is from their saying: "So-and-so eats from a trade (ḥirfa) that he practises and from a craft (ṣan'a) that he pursues," meaning: that is his sustenance and the direction from which he obtains his livelihood. It is as if He said: "These gardens are the means of your provision and your livelihood; from them you are provided for and you make your living."

﴿And a tree﴾ is coordinated with "gardens" (jannat), and it is the olive tree. ﴿That springs forth from Mount Sinai﴾. The phrase "Ṭūr Sīnāʾ" and "Ṭūr Sīnīn" cannot be otherwise: either the word ṭūr (mountain) is attached to a locality named Sīnāʾ or Sīnūn, or it is the name of the mountain, compounded of a mudaf and a mudaf ilayhi, like Imru' al-Qays. It is the mountain of Palestine. Sīnāʾ is in every case diptote (ghayr munṣarif), with a kasra on the sīn as in the reading of the Ḥijāzī (people) and Abū ʿAmr, for the definiteness and foreignness (ʿujma), or with a fatḥa on it as in the reading of the others, because the alif is the feminine marker, like ṣaḥrāʾ. ﴿Growing with oil﴾. Al-Zajjāj said: the bāʾ is for the state (ḥāl), meaning: it grows while the oil is with it. "Tunbitu" (it produces) is the reading of Makkī and Abū ʿAmr, either because anbata has the meaning of nabata, as in his saying: "until when the herbage has sprouted" (ḥattā idhā anbata al-baqlu); or because its object is omitted, meaning: it produces its olives, and in it is the oil. ﴿And a condiment for the eaters﴾, that is, a relish (idām) for them. Muqatil said: God, exalted is He, made in it both relish and oil; so the relish is the olive and the oil is the olive oil. (p-464) It is said that it is the first tree that grew after the Flood. He singled out these three kinds because they are the noblest of trees, the best of them, and the most comprehensive of benefits.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 21:

﴿And indeed, for you in the cattle there is a lesson﴾. Al-An'am is the plural of na'am, and it refers to camels, cattle and sheep. ﴿We give you to drink﴾. With the letter nun vowelled with a fatha, this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami), Nafi' and Abu Bakr. Saqa (to give to drink) and asqa (to give to drink) are two dialectal forms of the same meaning. ﴿From what is in their bellies﴾, i.e., We bring out for you from their bellies milk that is pure and easy to drink. ﴿And for you in them are many benefits﴾, besides the milk, and these are the benefits of their wool, fur and hair. ﴿And from them you eat﴾, i.e., from their flesh.

**﴿And upon them﴾** — i.e., upon the livestock on land, **﴿and upon the ships﴾** — on the sea, **﴿you are carried﴾** — on your journeys.

This indicates that by "the livestock" (al-an'am) is meant the camels (al-ibil), because they are the animals that are normally ridden upon. Therefore it paired them with "the ships" (al-fulk), which are the vessels (al-safa'in), since camels are the "ships of the land." Dhu al-Rummah said:

﻿"…… a ship of the land, its reins beneath my cheek"

He means his she-camel.

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah"﴾ (make Him one) ﴿"You have no god other than Him"﴾ (no deity worthy of worship) ﴿other than Him﴾ is read in the nominative on the basis of the *mahall* (grammatical position) and in the genitive on the basis of the *lafz* (wording). The clause is a *isti'naf* (resumptive, independent sentence) that serves as a *ta'lil* (causal justification) for the command to worship. ﴿"Will you not then fear God?"﴾ (Will you not fear the punishment of Allah, who is your Lord and your Creator, if you worship other than Him, something that has no claim whatsoever to being worshipped?)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 24:

﴿So the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said﴾

﴿So the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said﴾ That is: their notables, to their common folk, ﴿"This is none but a mortal like yourselves, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink"﴾, ﴿"wishing to make himself superior over you"﴾, that is, seeking superiority over you and (p-465) seeking to lead you. ﴿"Had Allah willed [to send a messenger], He would surely have sent down angels"﴾, that is, He would surely have sent angels. ﴿"We never heard of this among our forefathers of old."﴾ That is: of the sending of a human being as a messenger, or of what he commands us concerning monotheism and reviling our gods. And the strange thing about them is that they accepted divinity for a stone but did not accept prophethood for a human being.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 25:

﴿He is nothing but a man in whom there is madness (jinnah)﴾, that is, insanity (junun). ﴿So wait for him for a while﴾: await and be patient with him for a time, until his matter becomes clear. If he recovers from his madness, well; otherwise, you may kill him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 26:

﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, because they have denied me."﴾ When he despaired of their faith, he prayed to God for vengeance upon them. The meaning is: destroy them because of their denial of me, since in helping him lies their destruction. Or, "help me" replaces "because they have denied me," like your saying "this in place of that" (hadha bi-dhak), meaning: in place of that. The meaning is: replace for me the grief of their denial with the consolation of victory over them.

**Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, on Surah 23, verse 27:**

﴿So We revealed to him﴾, meaning: We answered his supplication, and so We revealed to him ﴿that he should build the ark under Our eyes﴾, meaning: you shall make it while you are confident of God's protection of you and His seeing you, or under Our protection and safeguarding, as if with you from God were guardians who watch over you with their eyes, lest an enemy confront you or any corrupter spoil your work. From this comes their saying: "Upon him is a watchful eye from God" (*ʿayn kāliʾah*). ﴿And by Our revelation﴾, meaning: Our command and Our teaching you how to make it. It is related that he was revealed to make it in the form of the breast of a bird (*juʾjuʾ al-ṭāʾir*). ﴿When Our command comes﴾, meaning: Our punishment, by Our order, ﴿and the oven gushes forth﴾, meaning: water welled up from the oven of bread, that is, the cause of the drowning was brought forth from the place of burning, so that it would be more forceful as a warning and a lesson. It is related that it was said to Noah: "When you see the water boiling up from the oven, board the ship, you and those who are with you." When the water gushed from the oven, his wife informed him, and he boarded. That oven was the oven of Adam; it passed on to Noah. It was made of stone. Its location is disputed: it is said to be in the mosque of Kufa, it is said to be in al-Sham, and it is said to be in India.

﴿Then load therein﴾, meaning: enter (*fa-adkhil*) into the ship ﴿of every pair, two﴾, meaning: from every kind, two pairs, namely the species of the male and the species of the female, such as camels, she-camels, horses and mares. ﴿Two﴾, meaning: two single ones, paired, such as the male camel and the she-camel, the stallion and the mare. It is related that he carried only that which gives birth or lays eggs.

﴿Of every﴾: Ḥafṣ (reads it as) ﴿kullin﴾, meaning: of every kind, ﴿two pairs, two﴾. The word *ithnayn* (two) is for emphasis and added clarification. ﴿And your family﴾, meaning your wives, your children, ﴿except those against whom the word has already gone forth﴾ from God, concerning their destruction, and they were his son and one of his two wives. Here *ʿalā* is used with what harms (*al-ḍārr*), just as *al-lām* is used with what benefits (*al-nāfiʿ*) in His saying: ﴿And indeed Our word has preceded for Our servants, the messengers﴾ [37:171], and similar to it: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾ [2:286]. ﴿And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned﴾, meaning: do not ask Me to save those who disbelieved, for I am drowning them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 28:

﴿Then when you and those with you have settled upon the ship﴾, then when you have become firmly established upon it as riders, ﴿then say: "All praise is due to Allah, who has delivered us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ He was commanded to praise Allah for their destruction and for the deliverance from them, and He did not say "then say" in the plural, although ﴿when you and those with you have settled﴾ carries the meaning of "when you (plural) have settled," because he is their prophet and their imam, so his saying is their saying. Along with this is the indication of the excellence of prophethood.

ﷺ is not present here; no honorific needed. Translating the passage.

﴿And say﴾ when you have boarded the ship, or when you have disembarked from it: ﴿"My Lord, cause me to alight at a blessed place, and You are the best of those who cause to alight."﴾ That is, an act of alighting (inzāl), or a place of alighting. "Manzilan" (a place to alight) — Abū Bakr [reads it] — meaning: a place. ﴿Blessed﴾ — and the blessing in the ship is deliverance (najāh) therein, and after disembarking from it, abundance of offspring and the successive arrival of good things.

Indeed in that (what was done to Noah and his people) are surely signs (lessons and admonitions). And indeed (here it is the lightened form of the heavy one, and the lam is the distinguishing particle between it and the negative), and the meaning is: indeed the matter and the story were that We were (surely) afflicting the people of Noah with a great trial and severe punishment, or testing Our servants by these signs, so that We might see who takes heed and remembers, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have left it as a sign, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ [al-Qamar: 15]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 31:

﴿Then We produced﴾ — created — ﴿after them﴾ — after the people of Noah — ﴿another generation﴾. They were ʿAd and the people of Hud. This is supported by the words of Hud: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 69]. And the account of Hud comes directly after the account of Noah in al-Aʿraf, Hud, and al-Shuʿara'.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 32:**

﴿So We sent among them﴾ The verb *al-irsal* (sending) is normally transitive with *ila* (to), but here and in His saying ﴿Thus We have sent you among a community﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30] and ﴿We did not send into any town﴾ [al-A'raf: 94], it is used with *fi* (in). However, the community and the town have been made the place of the sending, as in the verse of Ru'ba:

*I sent in them Mus'ab, the one of much hardship…*

﴿a messenger﴾ who was Hud, ﴿from among them﴾, from their own people, ﴿[saying]: "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary [of Him]?"﴾ *An* (that) is explanatory (*mufassira*) for *arsalna* (We sent), meaning: We said to them through the tongue of the Messenger, "Worship Allah."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 33:

﴿And the chiefs of his people said, those who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ He mentions the statement of the people of Hud in his reply in al-A'raf, where it is without a waw (wa), because it is in the sense of the answer to a questioner who says: "What did his people say?" and so it is said to him: "They said such and such." Here, however, it is with the waw, because it is a conjunction of what they said to what the Messenger said. Its meaning: there came together in attainment this truth and this falsehood. It is not an answer to the Prophet ﷺ connected to his speech, and it was not with the fa' (fa'). The fa' was used in the story of Nuh, because it is an answer to his saying, occurring immediately after it. ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾ is an attribute of "the chiefs" or of "his people." ﴿And denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ (p-468) i.e., the meeting of what is in it of reckoning, reward, punishment and other than that. ﴿And We had given them luxury﴾ and made them comfortable ﴿in the life of this world﴾ with abundance of wealth and children. ﴿This is not﴾ i.e., the Prophet, ﴿but a human like you, who eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ i.e., of it, so it was elided because of what precedes it, meaning: how can he claim the Messengership of God from among you when he is like you?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 34:

﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves﴾ — that is, in what he commands you and forbids you. ﴿Then you would surely be losers﴾ — the phrase "إنَّكم إذًا" (innakum idhan, "then indeed you") stands as the answer to the conditional clause and is a response to those among their people who said this to them, ﴿losers﴾ — by submitting to one like yourselves. And from their foolishness is that they refused to follow one of their own kind, yet worshipped one weaker than themselves.

﴿Ayaʿidukum annakum idhā mitum﴾ (with kasra on the hamza of inna): Nafiʿ, Hamza, ʿAli and Hafs read it with a kasra, and others with a damma. ﴿wa-kuntum turāban wa-ʿiẓāman annakum mukhrajūn﴾ (they will be raised) for questioning, reckoning, reward and punishment. The second "annakum" is repeated for emphasis, and this is acceptable because the adverbial phrase separates the first from the second. "Mukhrajūn" is the predicate of the first (annakum), and the sense is: "Does he promise you that when you have died and have become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?"

﴿Far, far is it﴾. With a kasra on the taa': Yazid [recited it so]. It is also reported from him with a kasra and tanwin (nunation) on both. Al-Kisa'i stops on the ha' (هَيْهاه), while others stop on the taa' (هَيْهات). It is an *ism al-fi'l* (a noun functioning as a verb) occupying the position of "بَعُدَ" (bo'ida, "was far"), whose agent is an implied pronoun. The meaning is: "Far is what you are promised of resurrection (al-ba'th)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 37:

﴿Not is it﴾ (*in hiya*). This is a *damir* (pronoun) whose referent is not known except from what follows it as its explanation. Its underlying form is *in al-hayat* (not is the life), ﴿except our life of this world﴾ (Al-An'am: 29). Then *hiya* was placed in the position of *al-hayat* (the life), because the predicate indicates it and makes it clear. The meaning is: there is no life except this life in which we are and which is near to us, and this. This is because the negating *in* (*in al-nafiyah*) entered upon *hiya*, which carries the sense of *al-hayat* and denotes the genus, so it negated it. Thus it is equivalent to *la* (*la al-lati li-nafy al-jins*), which is used to negate the genus.

﴿We die and we live﴾: meaning, some die and some are born; one generation passes away and another generation comes. Or there is an inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in it, meaning: we live and we die. This is the recitation of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

﴿And we are not those who will be resurrected﴾ after death.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 38:

﴿He is but a man who has fabricated against Allah a lie.﴾ That is: he is only one who fabricates against Allah, in what he claims of being sent as a prophet by Him, and in what he promises us of resurrection (al-ba'th). ﴿And we are not believers in him﴾, meaning: we are not those who confirm him.
﴿He said, "My Lord, support me, for they have denied me."﴾ So Allah answered the supplication of the Messenger with His saying:

﴿Qala ʿammā qalīlin﴾ — "mā" is either superfluous (zāʾida) or means "a thing" (shayʾ) or "a time" (zaman), and "qalīl" is a substitute (badal) for it. The response (jawāb) of the omitted oath (qasam) is ﴿la-yuṣbiḥunna nādimīn﴾, meaning: they will surely become regretful when they witness what will befall them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 41:

﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, i.e., the cry of Jibril. He shouted at them and so destroyed them. ﴿in truth﴾, i.e., with justice from Allah. It is said, "So-and-so judges with truth," meaning with justice. ﴿So We made them into debris﴾. He likened them, in their destruction, to ghuthaʾ (debris, ghuthaʾ), which is the refuse carried by a torrent, of what has decayed and blackened from leaves and dry stalks. ﴿So away with them﴾, i.e., destruction. It is said, "baʿida baʿadan wa buʿdan," meaning he perished. It is one of the verbal nouns (masadir) put in the accusative by verbs which are not used in their overt form. ﴿for the wrongdoing people﴾ is an explanation of those against whom the curse of "away" (buʿd) is invoked, like ﴿Hayta laka﴾ [Yusuf: 23].
Then We brought into being after them other generations (qurun), namely the people of Salih, Lut, Shu'ayb, and others.

Qur'anic quotations and the grammatical discussion are included below.

﴿No nation can precede its term﴾ "Min" (مِن) here is redundant (ṣilah), meaning: no nation precedes its term (ajal), the appointed time written for it and the moment set for its destruction and decreed. ﴿Nor can they delay it﴾ means they do not fall behind it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 44:

﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession.﴾ "Tatra" is on the pattern "fa'lā" (fa'lā). The alif is for the feminine, like "sakrā" (sukrā, intoxication), because "al-rusul" (the messengers) is a collective noun, and therefore it is not given tanwin, since it is diptote (ghayr munsarif). "Tatran" with tanwin is read by Makki and Abu 'Amr and Yazid, on the basis that the alif is for ilhaq (extension of a triliteral root to a quadriliteral pattern), like "arṭan" (a type of shrub). In both readings it is accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl): (p-470) meaning "consecutively, one after another." Its ta' in both readings is a substitute (badal) for the waw, and the original form is "witrā," from "witr" (odd, single), so the waw was changed to ta' as in "turāth" (inheritance).

﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him.﴾ The messenger is connected to both the sender and the one to whom he is sent, and the idafa (genitive construction) is by way of such connection, so its attribution to both is correct.

﴿So We made them follow one another﴾ — the nations and generations — ﴿one after another﴾ in destruction, ﴿and We made them into tales﴾ — reports that are heard and wondered at. "Ahadith" (tales) may be a collective noun for "hadith" (report), from which comes "ahadith of the Prophet" (ﷺ); and it may be the plural of "uhdutha" (a tale), which is what people talk about for amusement and wonder, and this is the meaning intended here.

﴿So away with a people who do not believe.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 45:

﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun﴾ — "Harun" is a substitute (badal) for "his brother" — ﴿with Our signs﴾, the nine (clear signs) — ﴿and a manifest authority﴾, and a plain proof.
To Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they became arrogant: they refused to accept faith out of haughtiness and self-exaltation. ﴿And they were a haughty people﴾, domineering and overbearing.

"So they said: 'Shall we believe in two humans like ourselves?'" (﴿فَقالُوا أنُؤْمِنُ لِبَشَرَيْنِ مِثْلِنا﴾)

Al-Basharu (the human being) is used both in the singular and the plural. Mithl (like) and ghayr (other) are words by which two persons, a group, a masculine and a feminine may all be described.

"And their people" (﴿وَقَوْمُهُما﴾), i.e., the Children of Israel, "are our worshippers" (﴿لَنا عابِدُونَ﴾), meaning: submissive and obedient. Among the Arabs, anyone who submits to a king is considered his ʿābid (worshipper, i.e., servant) of him.
﴿So they denied them, and they became among those destroyed﴾ by drowning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 49:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾ — that is, to the people of Musa — ﴿the Torah﴾ — ﴿that perhaps they may be guided﴾ — that they may act upon its laws (shara'i') and its admonitions (mawa'iz).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 50:

﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾ indicating Our power over whatever We will, because he was created without a father's sperm-drop. [The verb] "wahhada" (made it singular) is used because the wonder in both of them is one. Or the intended meaning is: "And We made the son of Maryam a sign and his mother a sign," and the first [sign] is elided because the second points to it. ﴿And We sheltered them﴾, i.e., We made (p-471) their refuge, that is, their dwelling-place, ﴿on a high ground﴾. Shami and Asim [read] "rubwatin" (with a dammah on the ra'), while the others [read] "ribwatin" (with a kasra), meaning: a raised land. It is Bayt al-Maqdis, or Damascus, or al-Ramla, or Egypt. ﴿Possessing a resting-place﴾, a settled place of level, spread-out land, or possessing fruits and water, meaning: because of the fruits, its inhabitants settle there. ﴿And a spring﴾, and apparent running water upon the face of the earth. It is a maf'ul (passive participle), i.e., "perceived by the eye" by its manifestness, from "ana-hu" (when he perceived it with his eye); or it is a fa'il (active form), in that it is beneficial by its manifestness and its flowing, from "al-ma'un," which is benefit.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 51:

﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things﴾. This address and this speech are not to be taken in their apparent sense, because the messengers were sent separately, at different times. The meaning is rather to inform that each messenger, in his own time, was addressed with this and enjoined with it, so that the listener may believe that a command which all the messengers were addressed with and enjoined with is truly deserving of being taken up and acted upon. Or it is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ), on account of his excellence and his standing in place of all of them in his time, and he used to eat from the spoils of war. Or it is an address to ʿIsa (ʿalayhi al-salam), because the verse is connected with mention of him, and he used to eat from the spinning of his mother, and that is the best of good things. What is meant by "the good things" is that which is lawful (ḥalal), and the command is for obligation (taklif). Or it means what is pleasant and enjoyable, and the command is for indulgence and permissibility.

﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ conforming to the Shariʿa (ʿamal ṣāliḥ: righteous action; sharīʿa: the divine law).

﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾, so I will reward you for your deeds.

﴿And indeed this﴾ is read by the Kufans as a resumptive sentence (al-istinaf, a new clause that begins a fresh statement). "Wa-anna" (with a fatha on the hamza) is read by the Hijazis and the Basrans with the meaning of "wa-li-anna" ("and because"), so that the sense is: "﴿so fear Me﴾ because this..." Alternatively, it is coordinated with what precedes it, so that the sense is: "﴿I am fully aware of what you do﴾, and [I am aware] that this..." Or its implied form is: "Know that this..." ﴿Your community﴾ means your religion (milla) and your sacred law (shari'a) which you follow. ﴿One community﴾ means one religion, which is the sacred law of Islam. "Ummatan" (as a community) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). The meaning is: indeed the religion is one religion, which is Islam, and similar to it is the verse ﴿Indeed the religion with Allah is Islam﴾. ﴿And I am your Lord﴾ alone, ﴿so fear Me﴾, that is, fear My punishment for opposing My command.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 53:

﴿Then they broke their affair into sects among themselves.﴾ Taqatta'a (تَقَطَّعَ) is used in the sense of qatta'a (قَطَّعَ), i.e., they divided the affair of their religion (قَطَّعُوا أمْرَ دِينِهِمْ) (p-472) ﴿into scriptures (zuburan)﴾, the plural of zabur (زَبُورٍ), i.e., different books; meaning, they made their religion into religions. It has also been said: they split into sects in their religion, each sect adopting a book (تَنْتَحِلُ كِتابًا). And from al-Hasan: they tore the Book of Allah into pieces (قِطَعًا) and distorted it. It is also read "zubaran" (زُبَرًا), the plural of zubrah (زُبْرَةٍ), i.e., pieces. ﴿Every party﴾: every sect of these divergent people who had split their religion ﴿with what they have﴾: of the Book and the religion, or of desire and opinion, ﴿rejoicing﴾: pleased, believing that they are upon the truth.
﴿So leave them in their confusion﴾ (ghamrah), i.e., their ignorance and heedlessness, ﴿until a time﴾, i.e., until they are killed or die.
﴿Do they think that what We provide them with of wealth and children﴾. *Ma* here has the sense of *alladhi* (the one which), and the *khabar* (predicate) of *anna* (that)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 56:

﴿We hasten to them with good things﴾. The pronoun returning from the predicate of inna to its subject is omitted; the sense is: "We hasten to them with it" (bihi). The meaning is: this provision is nothing but a means of gradual lure (istidraj) for them toward acts of disobedience, while they suppose it to be a hastening for them in good things and a speedy reward for their good conduct. This verse is a proof against the Mu'tazilah in the matter of al-aslah (what is most beneficial), for they say that God does not do to any of the creatures except what is most beneficial for them in religion, and He has informed that this is not good for them in religion, nor most beneficial. ﴿Rather they do not perceive﴾. Bal (rather) is a corrective (istidrak) to His saying ﴿Do they suppose...﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55]; that is, they are like beasts that have no awareness, so that they might reflect on this, that it is a gradual lure or a hastening in good.
Then He explained the mention of His friends (awliya') by saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive﴾. That is: fearful.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾ — that is, in all of God's Books; they do not distinguish between His Books, unlike those who "cut up their affair among themselves" (taqatta'u amrahum baynahum), and they are the People of the Book.
﴿And those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾ like the polytheists of the Arabs (p-٤٧٣)

﴿And those who give what they give﴾: that is, they give what they have given of zakat (obligatory almsgiving) and charities. It is also read as "yu'tūna mā atau" with qasr (the short, non-lengthened form), meaning they do what they did. ﴿And their hearts are fearful﴾: frightened that it will not be accepted from them because of their shortcomings, ﴿that they are returning to their Lord﴾. The majority hold that the estimate (taqdir, the supplying of an implied element) is "because they...", and the predicate of ﴿Indeed those who...﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57].

Those hasten towards the good things; they are eager for acts of obedience and so hurry to perform them. ﴿And they are foremost in them﴾, that is: for the sake of the good things they outstrip others to the Gardens; or, for their sake they have outstripped people.

We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity (wus'aha), that is, its ability (taqatuha). The meaning is that what the righteous are described as doing does not lie outside the limit of capacity and ability, and likewise everything He has imposed on His servants. This is a refutation of those who permitted the imposition of what cannot be borne (taklif ma la yutaq).

﴿And with Us is a Book which speaks with the truth, and they will not be wronged﴾: that is, the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) or the record of deeds (sahifat al-a'mal). On the Day of Resurrection they will read from it nothing but what is truthful and just, with no addition and no deficiency, and none of them will be wronged by an increase in punishment, a decrease in reward, or by being charged with what is beyond their capacity.

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿بَلْ قُلُوبُهم في غَمْرَةٍ مِن هَذا﴾ = "Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this."

Translation:

﴿Nay, their hearts are in confusion about this.﴾ Rather, the hearts of the disbelievers are in a heedlessness that engulfs them, from which those described here among the believers are free. ﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾, i.e., they have evil deeds that exceed and overstep that, i.e., what the believers were described with. ﴿They are doers of them﴾, and they persist in them, not weaned from them until Allah seizes them with punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 64:

﴿Until, when We seized their affluent ones﴾ (mutrafīhim, those made comfortable and luxurious) ﴿with the punishment﴾, the punishment of this world, which was famine for seven years when the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against them, or their being killed on the Day of Badr. Ḥattā (until) is the particle after which speech begins, and the speech is the conditional clause ﴿when they cry out﴾ (yajʾarūn), shouting (yaṣrukhūn) in appeal for help. Al-juʾār is shouting with an appeal for help. Then it is said to them (p-٤٧٤)
Do not cry out for help today; indeed, crying out will be of no benefit to you. ﴿Indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾ That is, from Our side no help or assistance will reach you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 66:

﴿Indeed, My verses were recited to you﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿but you used to turn back on your heels, retreating﴾, that is, you would go back backwards. Nukus (retreat) is to return backwards, and it is the most ugly of gaits, because one does not see what is behind him.

(Mustakbirin) proud, acting arrogantly towards the Muslims; it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to (tankisun) in verse 66. (Bihi) "by it": by the House (al-Bayt) or by the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), because they would say, "No one can prevail over us, for we are the people of the Haram." What permitted this pronominal reference (idmar) is that they were well known for their arrogance regarding the House, or, according to another reading, "by My signs" (bi-ayati), since these are in the sense of "My Book." The meaning of their arrogance regarding the Qur'an is their denial of it out of arrogance. (Mustakbirin) has been construed to carry the sense of (mukadhdhibin, "denying"), and so it takes the same complement; or the preposition (ba) is connected to the word (samiran). They would hold nocturnal gatherings (tasmurun), talking about the Qur'an and disparaging it, gathering around the House and conversing by night; most of their evening talk was mention of the Qur'an and calling it poetry and sorcery. (Samir) is, in general usage, like (hadir) in applying to a group, and it has been read as (summaran). Or it is connected to the word (tahjurun), which derives from (hujr), meaning raving nonsense. (Tahjirun) is the reading of Nafi', from (ahjara fi mantiqihi), meaning he spoke obscenely.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 68:

﴿Will they not then reflect upon the word?﴾ Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, so that they would know that it is the manifest truth, and thus believe in it and in the one who brought it? ﴿Or has there come to them that which did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ Rather, has there come to them that which did not come to their forefathers of old, and therefore they denied it and considered it an innovation?

Or did they not recognize their Messenger, so that they deny him?

Muhammad (ﷺ) with truthfulness, trustworthiness, soundness of intellect, purity of lineage, and good character; i.e., they knew him by these qualities, yet they deny him out of insolence and envy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 70:

﴿Or do they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ (It is) madness. But it is not so, for they know that he is the most sound of them in intellect and the most penetrating of them in understanding. ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾, the clear (ablaj) and the straight path, and that which opposes their desires and their whims, namely the Oneness of God (tawhid) and Islam. They found no way to refute it or repel it, so they attributed it to madness. ﴿And most of them are averse to the truth﴾. In this is evidence that the fewest of them were not averse to the truth; rather, they abstained from believing in it out of pride and disdain, and out of fear of the reproach of their people, who would say, "He has turned away (sabi'a)," and of abandoning the religion of their fathers, like Abu Talib.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 71:

﴿And if the Truth had followed their desires﴾, that is, Allah, ﴿their desires﴾ concerning what they believe of the gods, ﴿the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted﴾, as He said: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22], ﴿and whoever is in them﴾. He singled out the rational beings for mention, because others are subordinate to them. ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, with the Book which is their reminder, that is: their admonition or their honour, because the Messenger is from among them and the Qur'an is in their language; or with the reminder they used to wish for, saying: ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾, and so on. ﴿But they, from their reminder, are turning away﴾ through their own poor choice.

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment? But the payment of your Lord is better.﴾ Read by the people of Hijaz, Basra, and ʿĀṣim, with *kharjan… fakharju* (خَرْجًا.... فَخَرْجُ). Read by Shām (Syria) as *kharājan… fakharāju* (خَراجًا....فَخَراجُ), and by ʿAlī and Ḥamza. The *kharāj* (tax or levy) is what you pay to the imam from the zakat of your land, and to every worker from his wage and reward. The *kharj* (خَرْجُ) is more specific than the *kharāj*. You say *kharāj al-qaryah* (خَراجُ القَرْيَةِ, the tax of the village) and *kharj al-kurdah* (خَرْجُ الكُرْدَةِ). The addition of letters in the word indicates an addition in meaning, and for this reason the first reading is preferred. That is: "Or do you ask them, for your guidance of them, for a little of the gifts of the creatures? Then the abundance from the Creator is better." ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾, the most excellent of givers. (p-476)
Qur'anic verse: ﴿And indeed, you invite them to a straight path﴾ — and it is the religion of Islam; therefore it is fitting that they should respond to you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 74:

﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are certainly deviating from the path.﴾ They are certainly swerving away from this mentioned path, which is the straight path.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 75:

﴿Even if We had mercy on them and removed the harm that is upon them﴾ [when Allah had seized them with years of famine until they ate al-'ilhiz (a food made of blood and hair mixed together, eaten in famine)]. "Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: 'I implore you by Allah and by the ties of kinship. Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'You have killed the fathers with the sword and the sons with hunger.' So the verse was revealed."

The meaning: if Allah removed from them this harm, which is the drought that befell them, by His mercy toward them, and they found abundance, ﴿they would persist﴾, that is, ﴿they would continue in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾, meaning: they would return to what they had been upon of arrogance and enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and this humble submission before him would vanish from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 76:

﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves﴾ "Istakana" is of the form "istaf'ala" from "al-kawn" (being, state), meaning he passed from one state (kawn) to another, just as it is said "istaḥāla" when one passes from one condition (ḥāl) to another.

﴿حَتّى إذا فَتَحْنا﴾ "فَتَّحْنا" (with the doubled *ta*, *fattahna*) is the reading of Yazid (*Yazid*), ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ بابًا ذا عَذابٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾ "until when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment." That is, the gate of (p-477) hunger, which is more severe than captivity and killing. ﴿إذا هم فِيهِ مُبْلِسُونَ﴾ "then they are in it, despairing": bewildered, hopeless of every good. The most obstinate of them and the most stubborn in opposition came, so that he might win your sympathy, or We tested them with every trial of killing and hunger, yet no softness of submission was seen in them. They remained so until, when they were punished with the Fire of Hell, then they will despair, like His saying: ﴿وَيَوْمَ تَقُومُ الساعَةُ يُبْلِسُ المُجْرِمُونَ﴾ "And on the day the Hour arises, the criminals will despair" [al-Rum: 12].

Verse 78 of Surah 23 (al-Mu'minun): "It is He who produced for you hearing, sight and hearts (af'idah)." He singled these out for mention because they have, connected to them, religious and worldly benefits that are not connected to anything else. "Little is it that you give thanks." That is: you give little thanks. Here "ma" is an emphasizing addition (zā'idah li-l-ta'kid), in the sense of "truly," and the meaning is: you have not recognized the magnitude of these blessings, and you have put them to other than their proper uses. You did not employ your sight and hearing in the signs and acts of God, and you did not reflect with your hearts so as to recognize the Bestower; and you gave thanks to Him for nothing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 79:

﴿And it is He who created you (dhara'akum) on the earth﴾, He created you and dispersed you through procreation (al-tanasul), ﴿and to Him you will be gathered﴾, you will be assembled (tujma'un) on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal.

It is He who gives life and causes death. That is: He gives life to souls (nasam) by bringing them into existence, and causes them to die by annihilating them. ﴿And His is the alternation of night and day.﴾ That is: the coming of each one after the other, and their alternation in darkness and light, or in increase and decrease. This belongs to Him alone, and none other can control their turning. ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ So that you would recognise Our power over resurrection, or so that you would reason from the handiwork to the Maker and believe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 81:

﴿Nay, but they said﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah, ﴿the like of what the former ones said﴾, i.e., the disbelievers before them. Then he explained what they said with His words:

(p-478)
﴿They say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?"﴾ "مِتْنا" (mitnā) is read by Nafi', Hamza, Ali and Hafs.

"We were indeed promised this, we and our fathers, before" (ﷺ) — no, let me translate precisely.

﴿We have indeed been promised this, we and our fathers before.﴾ That is, the resurrection (al-Ba'th), ﴿before﴾ the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿This is nothing but the myths of the ancients.﴾ Asatir is the plural of istar, which is the plural of satr (line), and it means what the ancients wrote that has no reality. The plural of ustura (usṭūrah) is more appropriate.

Then He commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to establish the proof against the polytheists by His saying: ﴿Say: "To whom belong the earth and whatever is in it, if you should know?"﴾ For indeed they...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 85:

﴿They will say, "To Allah."﴾ Because they acknowledge that He is the Creator. Then, when they say this, ﴿Say, "Will you not then remember?"﴾ so that you know that the One who originated the earth and whatever is in it is able to restore creation, and that He is worthy of not having any of His creatures associated with Him in lordship. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ With the lightened form (al-takhfif), Hamzah, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ read it; with the doubled form (al-tashdid), others read it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 86–87:

﴿Say: "Whose is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Allah's." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ Will you not fear Him so that you do not associate partners with Him? Or: Will you not then be mindful of Him, in your denial of His power over resurrection, while you acknowledge His power over creating these things?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verses 86–87:

﴿Say: "Whose is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "Allah's." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ Will you not fear Him so that you do not associate partners with Him? Or: Will you not then be mindful of Him, in your denial of His power over resurrection, while you acknowledge His power over creating these things?

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 23, verse 88:**

﴿Say: In whose hand is the dominion of all things?﴾ *Malakut* (dominion, sovereignty) means *mulk* (kingship). The *waw* and the *ta'* in *malakut* are for intensification (*mubalaghah*), so they indicate the greatness of the dominion. ﴿He gives protection, and none can be given protection against Him, if you know.﴾ *Ajartu fulanan 'ala fulan* means: I rescued so-and-so from so-and-so and prevented him (from harm). The meaning is: He rescues whomever He wills from whomever He wills, and none can rescue anyone from Him. (p-٤٧٩)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 89:

﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Then how are you deluded?"﴾ You are deceived away from the truth, or away from His oneness and obedience to Him. The deceiver is Satan and the (base) desire (al-hawa).

The first "li-Allah" (to Allah) is by consensus (ijma'), since the question is "to whom?" So too the second and third, according to other than the people of Basra, in terms of meaning: because when you say, "Who is the lord of this?" its meaning is, "To whom does this belong?" and so the answer is "to so-and-so," like the saying of the poet:

When it is said, "Who is the lord of the villages and the towns, and the lord of the thoroughbred horses?" it is said, "To Khalid."

That is, to whom do the villages belong? And whoever reads it with the omission of the (lam) then it is according to the apparent (wording), because when you say, "Who is the lord of this?" its answer is "so-and-so."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 90:

﴿Rather, We have brought them the truth﴾, that ascribing a son to Him is impossible and that associating partners with Him is false. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ in their saying that God has taken a son and in their invoking of a partner. Then He emphasized their lying with His saying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 91:

﴿Allah has not taken any offspring﴾, because He is exalted above kind and species, and a man's offspring is of his own kind. ﴿And there was not with Him any god﴾, meaning there is no partner with Him in divinity. ﴿Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾, meaning each of the gods would have been independent with what he created, and would have exclusively controlled it, and the dominion of each one of them would have been distinct from the others. ﴿And some of them would have overcome others﴾, meaning some of them would have prevailed over others, just as you see the state of the kings of the world, whose realms are distinct while they contend with one another. When you see no trace of the distinctness of realms or of contention, then know that He is one God, in whose hand is the sovereignty (malakut) of everything. It is not said that "idhan" (otherwise/then) enters only upon a statement that is a conditional and its response; here, "ladhahaba" (would have taken away) occurs as both the conditional response and the answer, and no condition or question of a questioner precedes it, because the condition is elided, and its estimated form is: "Had there been with Him other gods," being indicated by "and there was not with Him any god." This is a reply to those among the polytheists who argued with him. ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾, of rivals and offspring.

﴿عالِمِ﴾ with the genitive ending (بِالجَرِّ) is an attribute (ṣifah, a descriptive adjective) of God. With the nominative ending (وبِالرَفْعِ), the Madani and Kufi readers, other than Hafs, read it as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical topic), so it means "He is the Knower of ﴿الغَيْبِ والشَهادَةِ﴾, the hidden and the witnessed," meaning the secret and the manifest. ﴿فَتَعالى عَمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ means "Exalted is He above what they associate with Him," meaning the idols and other things.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 93:

﴿Say: "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised,﴾ "in" (إمّا) and the "nun" (النُون) are emphatic particles; that is: "if it must be that You show me what You promise them of punishment in this world or in the Hereafter."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 94:

﴿My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people﴾. That is: do not make me a companion of theirs, and do not punish me with their punishment. From al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him): Allah informed him (the Prophet) that there would be a chastisement (niqmah) upon his community, but did not inform him when it would occur, so he was commanded to make this supplication. It is also permissible that the infallible Prophet (ﷺ) asks his Lord for what he knows He will do, and seeks refuge in Him from what he knows He will not do, as a demonstration of servitude (ubudiyyah) and humility before his Lord. His seeking forgiveness (istighfar) from him, peace be upon him, when he rose from his gathering seventy times for this reason is also related. The fa' in fa-la (فَلا) is the response to the conditional clause, and "Rabb" (رَبِّ) is a parenthetical insertion between them for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 95:

﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them.﴾ They used to deny the promise of punishment and mock it. So it was said to them: Indeed Allah is able to fulfil what He has promised, if you reflect—so what is the basis for this denial?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 96:

﴿Repel with that which is better﴾ with the trait which is ﴿better﴾, ﴿the evil﴾. It is more eloquent than saying "with the good, the evil," because of the detail it contains; it is as if he said, "Repel with the best (al-husna) the evil." The meaning is: pardon their harm and respond to it with as much goodness as possible. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. The evil is shirk, or foul speech repelled with peace, or the reprehensible repelled with admonition. It has been said that it is abrogated by the verse of the sword (naskh, abrogation, is the term for this view). It has also been said that it is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated), since conciliation (mudara) is encouraged so long as it does not lead to the breaching of religion. ﴿We are best aware of what they describe﴾ of shirk, or of their description of you and their evil speech, and We will recompense them for it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the promptings (hamazat) of the devils."﴾

"From their whisperings and their pricks." Al-hamz (هَمْز) means pricking (al-nakh), and hamazat is the plural of hamzah, meaning a single instance of it. From this comes mihmaz (مِهْمَاز), the goad of the horse-trainer. The meaning is that the devils urge people toward sins just as the trainer of a beast goads the animals to make them walk.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 98:

﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ This is a command to seek refuge from their prods (nakhasat) in the words of one who supplicates to his Lord, repeating his call, and to seek refuge from their being present with him at all, or during the recitation of the Qur'an, or at the moment of death (al-naza').

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 23, verse 99:

﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾. *Hatta* (until) relates to *yasifun* (they describe). That is: they will not cease to associate partners [with God] until the time of death arrives. Or: they will not cease to be in evil remembrance (*su' al-dhikr*) until this time. What lies between them is mentioned by way of *i'tiraD* (parenthetical insertion, interjected clause) and *ta'kid* (emphasis), for overlooking them, seeking God's help against Satan, lest He cause him to slip from forbearance (*hilm*) and incite him to take retribution against them. ﴿He says: My Lord, send me back﴾. That is: return me to the world. He addressed God with the plural form for glorification, like the address of kings.

﴿So that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind﴾: in the place I left behind, which is the world, because he left the world and went on to the Hereafter. Qatada said: he did not wish to return to his family or his clan, but only so that he might make up for what he neglected.

﴿Li'allī﴾ with the ya' silent (sākinat al-yā') is read by al-Kūfī (the reader of Kufa), Sahl and Ya'qub. ﴿Kallā﴾: a rebuke against seeking a return, a denial, and a declaring it unlikely. ﴿Innahā kalimatun﴾: the intended meaning of kalima (word) is a group of speech whose parts are connected to one another, namely his saying ﴿Rabbi-ārjiʿūn﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99] ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind﴾. ﴿Huwa qā'iluhā﴾: he is undoubtedly its speaker; he will not leave it alone nor remain silent about it, because regret and remorse have overwhelmed him. ﴿Wa min warā'ihim﴾: that is, before them, and the pronoun refers to the group. ﴿Barzakh﴾: a barrier between them and a return to the world. ﴿Ilā yawmi yub'athūn﴾: it is not meant that they will return on the Day of Resurrection; rather, this is a total despair, since it is known that there is no return after the resurrection except to the Hereafter. (p. 482)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 101:

﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown﴾ — it is said that this is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah). ﴿There will be no kinship between them that day﴾ — Abu Bakr (read it) with idgham (assimilation), because the two similar letters coalesce, even though they come from two words. He means: severance will take place between them where they scatter, rewarded and punished, and there will be no connection between them through kinship, since a man will flee from his brother, his mother, his father, his companion and his sons. Connection is only through deeds. ﴿Nor will they ask one another﴾ — a question of mutual connection, as they used to ask one another in the world, because each one is preoccupied with his own state and does not ask about his companion. There is no contradiction between this and His saying: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning each other﴾ [al-Saffat: 27], for the Resurrection has stages: in one stage the fear will intensify upon them, so they will not ask one another, and in another stage they will regain consciousness, so they will ask one another.

﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾: "mawāzīn" is the plural (jamʿ) of "mawzūn" (مَوْزُون), meaning the deeds that are weighed, namely the righteous deeds that have weight and value (wazn wa-qadr) with God, Exalted is He. This is based on His saying: ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf: 105]. ﴿Those are the ones who will be successful.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 103:

﴿And those whose scales are light﴾ with evil deeds. What is meant is the disbelievers. ﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾, meaning they were defrauded of them. ﴿In Hell they will abide forever﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿have lost their souls﴾. The substitute and the substituted have no grammatical place (mahall), because the relative clause (sila) has no grammatical place. Or it is a second predicate (khabar ba'd khabar) of "those" (ulaika), or it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada').

Translation:

﴿Talfahu﴾ means: it burns. ﴿The Fire scorches their faces, and they therein are grimacing﴾, scowling; and it is said to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 105:

﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ That is, the Qur'an. ﴿And you used to deny them.﴾ And you claimed that they were not from Allah, exalted is He.

"They will say: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us" — [ghalabat ʿalaynā] meaning it took possession of us — [shiqwatunā] (also read shaqāwatunā by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī), and both are verbal nouns (maṣdar), meaning: we became wretched by our evil deeds which we committed. The saying of the people of ta'wil (interpretation), that "what was written against us of wretchedness overcame us," is not sound, because He only writes what the servant does and what He knows he will choose, and He does not write other than what He knew he would choose; so the servant is not overcome or compelled in the act. This is because they say that statement only as an excuse for their own neglect in his command, so it is not fitting for them to seek an excuse for themselves for what proceeded from them. "And we were a people who went astray" from the truth and the right course."
Our Lord, bring us out of it" — that is, out of the Fire. "Then if we return" — to disbelief and denial — "then indeed we are wrongdoers" — against our own souls.

﴿He said, "Be silent therein"﴾: be silent with the silence of humiliation and abasement. ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾: about lifting the punishment from you, for it will not be lifted or lightened. It was said that this is the last word they speak there, and after it there is no speech except *shahīq* (a high-pitched, gasping groan) and *zafīr* (a low, wailing sigh).

"أنْ يَحْضُرُونِي" "ارْجِعُونِي" "وَلا تُكَلِّمُونِي": with the *yā'* (the final ī of the first-person pronoun) in both continuous recitation (*waṣl*) and pausal recitation (*waqf*). Ya'qub and others read them without the *yā'*.

﴿Innahu﴾ means: indeed, the matter and the affair ﴿was that a group of My servants used to say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful"﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 110:

﴿Then you took them for mockery﴾ is the second object (maf'ul thani). With a damma on the sin (sakhriyyan, read with ḍamm), it is read by Madani, Hamza and ʿAli; both forms are a verbal noun (masdar) of sakhira, like al-sukhr, except that the ya' of the relative ending (ya' al-nisba) adds intensity (mubalagha). It was said: they are the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them; and it was said: specifically the People of the Suffa (ahl al-Suffa). Its meaning: you took them as objects of ridicule (huzu'an), and you occupied yourselves with them while mocking (sakhirin). ﴿Until they made you forget﴾ by your preoccupation with them in that attribute, ﴿My remembrance﴾, so you abandoned it; that is, preoccupation with them was the cause of your forgetting My remembrance. ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾ in mockery of them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience﴾ — for their patience (bi-sabrihim). ﴿That they﴾ — i.e., because they ﴿are the triumphant ones﴾. It is also permissible that (anna) be a second object, i.e., "I have rewarded them today with their triumph," because jaza (to reward) is transitive to two objects, as in ﴿And He rewards them for what they patiently endured with a garden﴾ [al-Insan: 12].

"Innahum" — Hamza and Ali (read it) as a new sentence (ista'naf), i.e., "Indeed they are the triumphant ones, not you."

﴿He says﴾: that is, Allah, or the one commanded to question them from among the angels. "Say" (*qul*) is read as an imperative by Makki, Hamzah and Ali (Makki is a reader of the Qur'an in the recitational tradition, and Hamzah and Ali are also among the recognised readers, the *qurra'*). It is a command to Malik (the angel in charge of Hell) to ask them: ﴿How many years did you remain on the earth?﴾ "in the world" (*fi al-dunya*). "Years in number" (*'adad al-sinin*): that is, how many years in number you remained. Here كَمْ (*kam*, "how many") is in the accusative case, governed by لَبِثْتُمْ (*labithtum*, "you remained"), and عَدَدَ (*'adad*) is a specification (*tamyiz*, a noun that clarifies the vagueness of a number).

﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ They considered the duration of their stay in the world to be short, compared with their eternal abiding (khulud) and with the torment they were in. For the one who is being tested feels the days of his trial to be long, and considers short the days of ease that have passed over him. ﴿So ask those who count.﴾ That is, the reckoning (al-hisab), or the angels who count the lifespans and deeds of the servants. "Fasal" without hamza: Makki and Ali.

﴿He said: "You stayed only a little."﴾ That is, you did not stay long in the world. He rebuked them for their heedlessness, in which they had been. "Qul in" (قُلْ إنْ) is the reading of Hamza and Ali.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 115:

﴿Did you suppose that We created you without purpose﴾ (ʿabathan) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: playing (ʿābithīn), or it is an accusative of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: for the sake of play (lil-ʿabath). ﴿And that you would not be returned to Us﴾ — read with a fatḥah on the tā' and a kasrah on the jīm by Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Yaʿqūb. It is coordinated (maʿṭūf) either upon ﴿that We created you﴾ or upon ﴿without purpose﴾, meaning: for play, and that We would leave you without being returned. Rather, We created you for the sake of moral responsibility (taklīf), and then for your return from the abode of responsibility to the abode of recompense, so We reward the good-doer and punish the wrongdoer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 116:

﴿Exalted is Allah﴾ above creating in vain, ﴿the King, the Truth﴾ — the One to whom sovereignty is due, because everything is from Him and returns to Him; or, the Established who does not cease, and whose dominion does not cease. ﴿There is no god but He, the Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ The Throne is described as noble (karam), either because mercy descends from it, or because of its attribution to the Most Noble of the noble. It was also read anomalously (shādhdhan) with the nominative ﴿al-Karīm﴾ as an attribute of the Lord, exalted is He. (p-485)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 117:

﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof﴾: i.e., no argument ﴿concerning it﴾. The phrase "for which he has no proof" is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the condition and its response, like your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, though no one is more deserving of kindness than him, Allah will surely reward him." Or it is a necessary descriptive attribute (sifah lazimah) brought in for emphasis, like His words ﴿it flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]; it does not mean that among the gods there is something for which a proof could be established. ﴿Then his reckoning﴾: i.e., his recompense, and this is the response of the condition ﴿is with his Lord﴾: i.e., He will certainly recompense him. ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾. He made the opening of the surah ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] and its closing ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾. So how far apart is the opening from the closing. Then He taught us to ask for forgiveness and mercy with His words.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 23, verse 118:

﴿And say: My Lord, forgive and have mercy﴾, then He said ﴿and You are the best of the merciful﴾, because when His mercy reaches anyone, it suffices him from the mercy of others, while the mercy of others does not suffice him from His mercy.
